ndvi.name: Plant greenness
ndvi.short: How green and vigorous the crops are.
ndvi.description: NDVI measures greenness from the light leaves reflect. Near 1 is very green; near 0 is bare or dry soil.
ndvi.forCrops: If your area looks less green than other years in the same month, there may be drought, pests or bare soil.

soil-moisture.name: Soil moisture
soil-moisture.short: How much water there is where the roots are.
soil-moisture.description: Water in the top meter of soil, estimated with the SMAP satellite and a NASA model.
soil-moisture.forCrops: Dry soil before planting = better to wait or pick a drought-tolerant crop. Very wet = waterlogging risk.

rain.name: Daily rain
rain.short: How much it rained that day.
rain.description: Rain estimated by the GPM satellite constellation (IMERG product), in millimeters per day.
rain.forCrops: Use it to spot heavy storms (erosion risk) or weeks without rain (irrigation, planting).

lst-day.name: Daytime ground heat
lst-day.description: Land surface temperature measured by MODIS (not air temperature). Monthly average.
lst-day.forCrops: A very hot surface = more plant stress and more water loss. Covering the soil lowers it.

lst-night.name: Night cold
lst-night.description: Night-time land surface temperature (MODIS), monthly average. Helps spot frost-prone areas.
lst-night.forCrops: Nights near 0 °C at the surface = frost risk for sensitive crops.

evap.name: Water the field loses
evap.description: Water leaving soil and plants into the air, from the NASA MERRA-2 model. ECOSTRESS (more detailed) is not available as a layer: it will come from the backend.
evap.forCrops: If more water is lost than rains, the crop needs irrigation or cover that keeps moisture.
evap.note: Model data (MERRA-2), not a direct measurement.

groundwater.name: Groundwater
groundwater.short: Whether stored underground water goes up or down.
groundwater.description: Change in all stored water (soil, aquifers, snow) measured through gravity by GRACE and GRACE-FO, versus the 2004–2009 average.
groundwater.forCrops: Negative values growing year after year = deeper wells and more expensive irrigation.
groundwater.note: Data up to 2022 in this layer.

relief.name: Relief and slopes
relief.description: Shading computed from NASA SRTM elevation. Strongly shaded areas are slopes.
relief.forCrops: Steep slope + intense rain + bare soil = erosion. Cover crops and contour lines help.

ndvi.title: NDVI (greenness)
ndvi.simple: A number from 0 to 1 that says how green and vigorous plants are, measured by satellite.
ndvi.example: If your maize reads 0.8 in July it is lush; if it reads 0.3, it may lack water or have pests.

et.title: Evapotranspiration
et.simple: The water that leaves the field into the air: what evaporates from the soil plus what plants “sweat”.
et.example: In a hot, windy month a field can lose 5 mm of water a day, more than it rains.

soil-moisture.title: Soil moisture
soil-moisture.simple: How much water there is in the soil where the roots are. The SMAP satellite estimates it every day.
soil-moisture.example: If the soil is dry before planting, it is better to wait for rain or choose a drought-tolerant crop.

anomaly.title: Anomaly (more or less than normal)
anomaly.simple: The difference between this year and the average of many years for the same month.
anomaly.example: “August had 20% less rain than normal” means less water fell than in a typical August.

frost.title: Frost risk
frost.simple: The chance that the temperature drops below 0 °C and water on the leaves freezes.
frost.example: If April has frosty nights, an early bean planting can get burned.

water-balance.title: Water balance
water-balance.simple: The account between water that arrives (rain, irrigation) and water that leaves (evaporation, plants).
water-balance.example: If 40 mm falls in a month and the field loses 120 mm, the balance is negative: there is drought.

grace.title: Groundwater (GRACE)
grace.simple: The GRACE satellites measure changes in gravity to know whether stored underground water goes up or down.
grace.example: If it falls every year, wells get deeper and irrigation costs more.

satellite-vs-field.title: Satellite vs. field measurement
satellite-vs-field.simple: A satellite sees a large area and clouds can block it; a measurement on your farm is exact but from one point.
satellite-vs-field.example: The satellite may say “dry area” even if your plot next to the river is moist.

confidence.title: Confidence and uncertainty
confidence.simple: How sure we are about a value or a recommendation. Low confidence = use it with care.
confidence.example: “Low confidence” can be because we have no soil test from your farm.

rain.title: Rain from satellites
rain.simple: Rain estimated by the GPM satellite constellation, every half hour around the world.
rain.example: It tells you whether your area had heavy storms or weeks without rain.

lst.title: Surface temperature
lst.simple: How hot the ground or the plants are on top, not the air. The MODIS satellite measures it.
lst.example: Bare soil at noon can go above 50 °C; covered soil stays much cooler.

heat.title: Heat stress
heat.simple: When it is so hot that the plant stops growing well or loses flowers.
heat.example: More than 35 °C during maize flowering can lower the harvest.

slope.title: Slope and erosion
slope.simple: How steep the land is. On steep land, heavy rain washes the soil away.
slope.example: On a 30% slope without cover, one storm can carry off the fertile layer.

legume.title: Legume
legume.simple: Plants like beans, soybean or clover that take nitrogen from the air and leave it in the soil.
legume.example: After a bean harvest, maize needs less fertilizer.

cover-crop.title: Cover crop
cover-crop.simple: A crop planted to protect and feed the soil, not to sell.
cover-crop.example: Sowing oats or rye after harvest keeps the soil from being bare in winter.

deep-roots.title: Deep roots
deep-roots.simple: Plants whose roots go deep and bring up water and nutrients, and loosen the soil.
deep-roots.example: Forage radish breaks the hard layer and leaves channels for water.

drought-tolerant.title: Drought-tolerant crop
drought-tolerant.simple: A crop that survives weeks with little water without losing the whole harvest.
drought-tolerant.example: Sorghum and millet handle a dry summer better than maize.

ph.title: Soil pH
ph.simple: How acidic or alkaline the soil is, from 0 to 14. Most crops grow well between 5.5 and 7.5.
ph.example: At pH 5 beans fix little nitrogen; a bit of lime helps.

organic-matter.title: Organic matter
organic-matter.simple: Plant and animal remains that are now part of the soil. It holds water and feeds the soil.
organic-matter.example: Going from 2% to 3% organic matter helps the soil handle a short drought better.

intercropping.title: Intercropping
intercropping.simple: Growing two or more crops together, in the same field at the same time, so they help each other: one holds up, one feeds the soil, one covers the ground.
intercropping.example: In a milpa, beans climb the maize and squash covers the soil between the plants.

strata.title: Plant layers
strata.simple: Each plant uses a different height and root depth. Mixing layers makes better use of light, water and space, and plants compete less.
strata.example: Maize on top, beans climbing and squash at ground level; below, cassava takes water from deeper down.

workday.title: Workday
workday.simple: One day of work by one person on the farm. It helps compare how much work each crop needs.
workday.example: If beans need 85 workdays per hectare, that is 85 days of work for one person (or 17 days for 5 people).

break-even.title: Recovering the investment
break-even.simple: The year when what you earned with the change equals what you would have earned staying the same. Before that year, the change still owes you.
break-even.example: If you earn less in year 1 while learning and buying seed, but more afterwards, around year 3 you are even.

soil-loss.title: Soil loss (erosion)
soil-loss.simple: The top layer of soil, the most fertile, that rain carries away when the ground is bare. It forms very slowly: what goes in one storm takes years to come back.
soil-loss.example: Losing 1 mm of soil on one hectare is about 13 tonnes of earth.

wholesale-price.title: Wholesale price
wholesale-price.simple: What traders pay at big food markets such as Corabastos. Farmers usually get less, because transport and middlemen come in between.
wholesale-price.example: If plantain sells for $2,000 a kilo at the market, the farm may get $1,200 or $1,400.

price-volatility.title: Price volatility
price-volatility.simple: How much the price goes up and down from month to month. A very volatile price is riskier: you may harvest right when it is low.
price-volatility.example: Tomatoes can cost twice as much in March as in July; rice changes much less.

oversupply.title: Oversupply
oversupply.simple: When more produce arrives than people buy, and the price falls. It happens when many farmers plant the same crop because it sold well the year before.
oversupply.example: If everyone in the village plants onions because they sold well, harvesting at the same time can halve the price.

gross-income.title: Gross income
gross-income.simple: What you get for selling the harvest before paying for seed, fertilizer, labour and transport. It is not profit.
gross-income.example: 10 tonnes of plantain at $1,500 a kilo is $15 million in gross income; profit is what is left after costs.

risk-zone.title: Risk zone
risk-zone.simple: A place where weather or land are more likely to hurt the harvest: drought, waterlogging, heat or soil that is degrading. It comes from combining several satellite datasets.
risk-zone.example: A municipality in red for drought had less rain and drier soil than normal: it pays to save water and keep the soil covered.

land-state.title: Land state
land-state.simple: How the land looks from the satellite: healthy plants, stressed plants, bare soil or water on top.
land-state.example: A pasture that dries out and loses grass moves from “healthy” to “stressed” or to “bare soil”.

markov.title: State changes (Markov chain)
markov.simple: It counts how much land moved from one state to another between two dates. From that we estimate where the land is heading if nothing changes.
markov.example: If 20 of every 100 healthy hectares became “stressed”, the arrow from healthy to stressed says 20 %.

crop-vulnerability.title: Crop vulnerability
crop-vulnerability.simple: How easily the crop gets damaged by the weather: heat, drought, too much rain or frost.
crop-vulnerability.example: Maize at flowering during a heat wave with dry soil is very vulnerable: it can lose a good part of the harvest.

soil-health.title: Soil health
soil-health.simple: Healthy soil is alive: it has organic matter, holds water, lets roots in and doesn't wash away with the rain.
soil-health.example: Leaving crop residue, rotating with beans and not burning help the soil hold more water in a drought.

formula.title: How we rank the options
formula.step1: You choose how much each thing matters: a lot counts 5, some counts 3 and a little counts 1.
formula.step2: Each option has a 0–100 score per topic, built from NASA data and agronomic rules.
formula.step3: We multiply each score by its weight, add everything up and divide by the sum of the weights.
formula.equation: Score = sum of (weight × score) ÷ sum of weights
formula.notes: “Improve the soil” combines organic matter, nitrogen and pest break. We estimate “less work” from how many plantings per year the option needs.
formula.local: Changing priorities does not fetch data again: the math runs on your phone.

ndvi.name: Satellite vision
ndvi.title: Satellite vision
ndvi.task: Three plots have thirsty plants, but to the eye everything looks green. Turn on satellite vision and tap them.
ndvi.lensOn: Satellite vision on. Low numbers are thirsty plants.
ndvi.needLens: Your eyes can't tell the difference. Turn on satellite vision.
ndvi.found: Good! {value}: thirsty plants. {left, plural, one {# to go.} other {# to go.}}
ndvi.healthy: That one reads {value}: green, strong plants. Look for the low numbers.
ndvi.allFound: You found them! The satellite sees thirst before your eyes do.
ndvi.formula: NDVI = (infrared − red) ÷ (infrared + red). It goes from 0 to 1.
ndvi.lesson: A high NDVI, close to 1, means green, strong plants. A low one warns of thirst, pests or bare soil, often before you can see it.
ndvi.science: A healthy leaf absorbs red light and reflects a lot of near-infrared, a light your eyes can't see. MODIS measures it almost every day; Landsat and Sentinel (HLS) every few days, in more detail.

et.name: The field sweats
et.title: The field sweats
et.taskSources: Water leaves the field into the air. Tap the 2 places the vapor comes from.
et.taskMax: Now play with the weather: make the field lose as much water as possible.
et.taskProtect: You can't change the sun or the wind. What can you do so the field loses less water?
et.scene: Field with plants. It loses {amount} of water a day.
et.soilFound: Yes! The soil loses water: that is evaporation.
et.leavesFound: Yes! Plants sweat through their leaves: that is transpiration.
et.cloudWrong: The cloud brings water, it doesn't take it. Look lower.
et.meter: The field loses {amount} of water a day
et.maxDone: {amount} a day! With strong sun, wind and bare soil the field dries out fastest.
et.protectDone: That's it! With covered soil the field loses {amount} less each day.
et.lesson: Evapotranspiration is the water that leaves the field: what evaporates from the soil plus what the plants sweat. More sun, heat and wind raise it; covering the soil lowers it.
et.science: ECOSTRESS measures leaf temperature from the Space Station: a plant that transpires stays cool, and one that heats up is thirsty. MODIS estimates evapotranspiration every 8 days.

balance.name: The water account
balance.title: The water account
balance.task: What comes in minus what goes out. Keep the soil water in the green band and tap Done.

wet.name: rainy October
wet.intro: Now a rainy month. You start with your usual watering: do you need it?

balance.cover: Cover the soil: {amount} less goes out
balance.okRound: Just right! The roots have the water they need.
balance.dryHint: More water still goes out than comes in: the soil dries out. Irrigate a bit more or cover the soil.
balance.wetHint: Too much water comes in: the soil gets waterlogged, the roots drown and the rain washes the soil away. It already rained a lot: irrigate less.
balance.lesson: The water balance is what comes in (rain and irrigation) minus what goes out (evaporation and plants). Negative means drought; a big surplus means waterlogged soil.
balance.science: GPM IMERG estimates rain every half hour all over the world; ECOSTRESS and MODIS estimate evapotranspiration. Subtracting one from the other gives your area's water balance.

anomaly.name: Dry for whom?
anomaly.title: Dry for whom?
anomaly.task: Compare today's soil water with what is normal for that month in that place. How is it?

boyaca.why: It has 12 points less than normal: a dry anomaly.

guajira.why: There is very little water, but it is always like that there in March: no anomaly.

choco.why: There is plenty of water, but 12 points less than normal for Chocó: a dry anomaly.

llanos.why: It has 10 points more than normal: a wet anomaly. Watch out for waterlogging.

anomaly.formula: Anomaly = today's moisture − the average of many years in the same month.
anomaly.lesson: An anomaly compares with what is normal for each place and month. Little water is not always an anomaly, and a lot of water can be less than normal.
anomaly.science: SMAP measures the moisture of the top layer of soil with microwaves, even through clouds, every 2 or 3 days. The anomaly subtracts the average of many years for the same month.

frost.name: The coldest night
frost.title: The coldest night
frost.taskFind: Change the sky, the wind and the place. Find the night when frost falls.
frost.question: Tonight the forecast says clear sky and calm. Your beans are in the hollow. What do you do?
frost.scene: Night on the farm. At dawn: {temp}, {risk}.

why.clear: With no clouds, the soil's heat escapes to the sky and the night gets colder.
why.cloudy: Clouds are like a blanket: they keep the soil's heat in.
why.calm: With no wind, the cold air stays still, close to the ground.
why.windy: The wind mixes the air and doesn't let the cold settle.
why.hollow: Cold air is heavy: it flows down and pools in the hollow.
why.slope: On the slope the cold air drains downhill.

frost.found: There's the frost! Clear sky, no wind and in the hollow: the most dangerous night.

options.wait: Wait and see if there is ice at dawn
options.cover: Cover them with cloth before dark

feedback.wait: When you see the ice it's too late: frost burns the leaves before dawn.
feedback.cover: Good! The cloth keeps the soil's heat close to the plants.
feedback.fertilize: Fertilizer doesn't protect from cold. Look for something that keeps heat in.

frost.lesson: There is frost risk when the temperature near the ground drops below {zero}. Clear, windless nights and hollows are the most dangerous.
frost.science: On clear nights leaves can get up to {delta} colder than the air. NASA POWER gives each day's minimum temperature; MODIS measures surface temperature at night.

sensors.title: Soil detective
sensors.task: Mission: find the driest plot on the farm so you water it first.

now.look: Look at the farm from the satellite. Tap the green button.
now.seen: The satellite sees the whole farm as one single square: {value} water. It's an average: it doesn't say which plot is driest.
now.probe: {left, plural, =0 {Done.} one {Tap # more plot to place the last sensor.} other {Tap # plots, one by one, to place a sensor in each.}}
now.decide: Tap the plot with the lowest number: that's the driest.

sensors.probeTip: Tip: one near the river, one in the middle and one far away.
sensors.probeValue: Sensor: {value} water, exact for that plot.
sensors.combined: Map ready! The satellite gave the big picture and your sensors the detail.
sensors.decideOk: That's the one! The plot farthest from the river is the driest.
sensors.decideNo: That plot has {value}: others have less water. Look for the lowest number.
sensors.formula: Combined map: the satellite's pattern, adjusted with each sensor's exact value.
sensors.lesson: The satellite sees the whole area every day, but in big squares. A field sensor is exact, but at a single spot. Together they give a more accurate map of your farm.
sensors.science: SMAP measures moisture in squares several kilometres wide. Models use ground sensors to correct the satellite's error, and the satellite to estimate what happens between one sensor and the next.

season.name: Survive the season
season.title: Survive the season
season.task: 4 moments of the season. Read the satellite warning and choose what to do to look after your crop and your soil.
season.endTitle: This is how your season ended
season.endText: When heat rises, moisture drops and evaporation grows at the same time, the crop becomes vulnerable. Covered soil with rotation keeps more water and holds up better.

storm.title: Heavy downpour on freshly ploughed soil

options.cover: Leave crop residue or sow a cover crop

feedback.plow: Ploughing wet soil compacts it, and the next downpour carries the fertile soil away.
feedback.cover: Good! Roots and residue slow the water: the soil doesn't wash away.
feedback.nothing: Bare soil loses a bit of earth with every downpour.

say.ndvi: Greenness {value}: the soil has almost no plants covering it.

options.dawn: Irrigate at dawn and cover the soil

feedback.noon: It helps, but with so much heat a lot of water evaporates before it reaches the roots.
feedback.fertilize: With dry soil, fertilizer can burn the roots.
feedback.dawn: Good! Less evaporates at dawn and the cover keeps the moisture in.

say.temp: It's {value} right when the maize is flowering: very hot.
say.moisture: The soil has only {value} water: very dry.
say.et: The field loses {value} of water a day: it dries out fast.

options.scout: Go and look at that corner

feedback.spray: Without knowing the cause, the pesticide wastes money and harms soil life.
feedback.scout: Good! The satellite warns; your eyes confirm if it's water, pests or missing nutrients.
feedback.ignore: By the time the patch is visible to the eye, the damage has grown.

say.ndvi: In one corner of the plot greenness dropped to {value}: those plants are suffering.

harvest.title: You harvested the maize. What comes next?

feedback.repeat: Repeating the same crop tires the soil and helps pests.
feedback.burn: Burning destroys organic matter and leaves the soil bare against the rain.
feedback.legume: Good! Beans give nitrogen back to the soil and break the pest cycle.

say.ndvi: Greenness {value}: the maize was harvested and the soil is free.

season.lesson: Heat, soil moisture, rain, evaporation and greenness move together. When several go wrong at once the crop is more vulnerable; healthy, covered soil cushions the blow.
season.science: Satellites don't see your decisions, but they see their effects: SMAP sees moisture, GPM rain, ECOSTRESS evaporation and MODIS greenness. Together they show the risk before it shows on the plant.

about.title: About the data
about.intro: Field Shift combines NASA Earth observations with simple agronomic rules. Here is what we use, how often it updates and what it cannot tell you.
about.harmonize: Each dataset has its own grid and rhythm. For your farm we take the value of the pixel that covers it (or the average if it is large), turn it into monthly values and compare it with its own 20–25 year average. So a moisture anomaly means "drier or wetter than normal at that place", not an absolute number.
about.limitsTitle: What this data cannot tell you
limits: A pixel averages a large area (30 m to 50 km): it cannot see differences inside your field.
Clouds, snow or dense vegetation leave gaps or lower quality.
Data arrives days or weeks late: it is for trends, not for deciding today’s irrigation.
It does not replace a soil test or the experience of the people who work the land.
about.privacy: We use your connection to find your approximate area and, if you allow it, your phone’s GPS to be more precise. We do not store your location on our servers; your farms and preferences stay on this phone.
about.credits: Made by the Field Shift team for NASA Space Apps 2026 (Field Shift: Adapting Farms with NASA Data challenge). Maps: satellite imagery from Esri/MapTiler, labels from OpenFreeMap © OpenStreetMap contributors, NASA GIBS layers, Terrarium terrain (AWS Open Data), department and municipality boundaries from DANE (National Geostatistical Framework, via OCHA HDX). Place search: Nominatim/OpenStreetMap.
about.disclaimer: This tool supports, and does not replace, the farmer’s judgment or local advisors.

three-sisters.name: Three sisters (milpa)
three-sisters.story: A pairing from the peoples of Mesoamerica and North America: maize holds up, beans feed the soil and squash covers the ground.
three-sisters.layout: Plant maize in rows or mounds. When it is about 15 cm tall (about 3 weeks), sow 2 or 3 beans at the base of each plant and squash between the rows, every 1 to 2 m.

milpa-cassava.name: Milpa with cassava
milpa-cassava.story: A tropical version: cassava keeps growing for months after the maize, beans and squash are harvested.
milpa-cassava.layout: Plant cassava and maize on the same day, in alternating rows. After 3 weeks, beans at the base of the maize and squash in the open spaces. Cassava is harvested last.

cassava-groundnut.name: Cassava with groundnut
cassava-groundnut.story: Common in tropical America and Africa: groundnut covers and feeds the soil while cassava grows slowly.
cassava-groundnut.layout: Cassava every meter; between rows, 2 lines of groundnut. Groundnut is harvested at 4 months and cassava stays.

maize-pigeonpea.name: Maize with pigeon pea
maize-pigeonpea.story: Used in India and East Africa: pigeon pea grows slowly under the maize, stays after harvest and its roots go deep.
maize-pigeonpea.layout: Alternate 2 rows of maize and 1 of pigeon pea. After the maize harvest, pigeon pea keeps the soil covered.

millet-cowpea.name: Millet with cowpea
millet-cowpea.story: A Sahel classic: creeping cowpea covers the soil between the millet and feeds it.
millet-cowpea.layout: Sow millet with the first rains; about 2 weeks later, cowpea between the plants.

sorghum-pigeonpea.name: Sorghum with pigeon pea
sorghum-pigeonpea.story: Common in dry parts of India: two drought-tolerant crops with roots at different depths.
sorghum-pigeonpea.layout: 2 rows of sorghum and 1 of pigeon pea. Sorghum is harvested first and pigeon pea stays.

coffee-agroforestry.name: Coffee with plantain and shade trees
coffee-agroforestry.story: An agroforestry system: trees and plantain give shade, and forage peanut covers the soil all year.
coffee-agroforestry.layout: Plantain every 2 or 3 rows of coffee and leguminous shade trees (such as Inga) every 10 to 12 m. Forage peanut between the rows.

maize-soybean-strips.name: Maize and soybean strips
maize-soybean-strips.story: Alternating strips: soybean feeds the soil and maize does not shade it too much if the strips are wide.
maize-soybean-strips.layout: Strips of 4 to 6 rows of maize and 4 to 6 of soybean, running north to south.

winter-cover-mix.name: Rye, vetch and radish cover mix
winter-cover-mix.story: For the cool season between harvests: rye protects, vetch feeds the soil and radish loosens it.
winter-cover-mix.layout: Broadcast or drill it after harvest. End it 2 or 3 weeks before the next planting.

oats-vetch.name: Oats with vetch
oats-vetch.story: Cool-season forage or cover: vetch climbs the oats and leaves nitrogen behind.

formula.title: How do we calculate this?
formula.climate: Fits your climate: we look for the best planting month using NASA POWER temperature, frost and rain. The crop that does worst counts the most.
formula.synergy: Help each other: each pair adds points if one holds up, feeds, covers or shades the other, and loses points if they share pests, block each other's light or compete for fertilizer. Well-known pairings (like the milpa) count double.
formula.space: Heights and roots: how much of the space from the ground to the tallest plant has leaves, how much of the soil the roots reach, and whether the cycles have different lengths.
formula.soil: Care for the soil: adds points for a legume, for covering the soil (more if your field has erosion risk) and for deep roots.
formula.fit: Fits your farm: what you told us (your last crop, fertilizer, pests, what the harvest is for), your markets and the workload.
formula.total: Total: a weighted average. Climate weighs 3 (4 if saving water matters a lot to you), helping each other and heights weigh 2, soil weighs more if soil or erosion matter to you, and your farm weighs 2 if you answered the land questions.
formula.limits: These are general rules with typical values for each crop. They do not know your variety, your exact soil or your prices.
